                            SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-16349
                               PUC DOCKET NO. 59475

JOINT APPLICATION OF ONCOR                    §
ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY                     §
LLC AND LCRA TRANSMISSION                     §
SERVICES CORPORATION TO                       §
AMEND THEIR CERTIFICATES OF                   §
CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY                     §    BEFORE THE STATE OFFICE

SWITCH TO BIG HILL SUBSTATION                 §                   OF
765-KV TRANSMISSION LINE                      §
PROJECT IN BELL, BURNET,                      §    ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS
CONCHO, CORYELL, LAMPASAS,                    §
LLANO, MASON, MCCULLOCH,                      §
MENARD, MILAM, MILLS, SAN SABA,               §
SCHLEICHER, TOM GREEN, AND                    §
WILLIAMSON COUNTIES                           §

             THE MEWHINNEY FAMILY’S REPLY TO EXCEPTIONS TO
                      THE PROPOSAL FOR DECISION

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES AND COMMISSIONERS OF
THE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS:

        Ann Mewhinney Matous, Kate Richter Brown, Suzanna Richter, Mary Mewhinney

 Smith, Madison Goodman, Connor Smith, Miranda Smith, the Ann Mewhinney Irrevocable

 Ranch Trust 2024, the Mary Mewhinney Irrevocable Ranch Trust 2025, and Cathey Creek

 Limited (collectively, the “Mewhinney Family”) timely file this Reply to Exceptions to the

 Proposal for Decision (“PFD”) issued August 20, 2026. The Public Utility Commission of

 Texas (“Commission” or “PUC”) and Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA

 Transmission Services Corporation (collectively, “Applicants”) filed exceptions to the PFD on

 September 2, 2026, respectively. For the reasons stated below, the Mewhinney Family

 respectfully requests that the Commission reject those exceptions. The record supports the

 Administrative Law Judges (“ALJs”)’ recommendation to deny the Applicants’ Joint



                                               1
     Application to Amend their Certificates of Convenience and Necessity for the Bell County

    East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765-kV Transmission Line Project (“Application”).

    I.   Reply to Exceptions to Findings of Noncompliance with Notice Requirements

         A.       The Commission Staff’s position on Notice Requirements under 16 TAC
                  § 22.52(a)(3)

                  1.       There is no rule language linking the word “current” in 16 TAC § 22.52

                           (a)(3) to the filing date of the application.1

                  2.       The PFD’s interpretation of the rule is “unworkable because notice of the

                           application was provided to thousands of landowners, and the notice

                           packet is “nearly 100 pages long” therefore making it unreasonable for

                           the Applicants to prepare notice documents in a single day. Further,

                           Commission Staff notes that the PFD’s interpretation “may entail a lesser

                           burden for smaller applications, the compliance obligation becomes

                           impractical for an application that spans fifteen counties.” 2

         B.       The Mewhinney Family’s Reply

         Procedural due process under the Texas Constitution’s Due Course of Law clause

requires notice and a meaningful opportunity to be heard that is commensurate with the scale,

complexity, and private property interests at stake. When a regulatory agency reviews a project

of completely unprecedented scale, the standard for what constitutes “adequate notice” and

“sufficient time to prepare” must scale proportionally.3 The current docket contemplates a



1
  Commission Staff’s Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision at 5.
2
  Id.at 6.
3
  Tex. Const. art. I, § 19.2.; Univ. of Tex. Med. Sch. at Houston v. Than, 901 S.W.2d 926, 930 (Tex. 1995) (finding
that the process due must provide "notice and a meaningful opportunity to be heard," and that these safeguards must
be measured by "the nature of the proceeding and the "interests at stake"); B. Gregg Price, P.C. v. Series 1 - Virage
Master LP, 661 S.W.3d 419, 423 (Tex. 2023) (reaffirmation stating that both the U.S. and Texas Constitutions mandate
that any deprivation of property by adjudication “be preceded by notice and opportunity for hearing appropriate to the

                                                          2
 massive, state-wide buildout of 765-kilovolt (kV) extra-high-voltage transmission lines under

the umbrella of the Permian Basin Reliability Plan—a multi-billion dollar project impacting

thousands of acres of private property, historical sites, and agricultural land. To force newly

affected landowners to evaluate complex routing options and formulate formal legal responses

within a highly compressed, fast-tracked administrative window creates an unconstitutional risk

of erroneous deprivation.

         Furthermore, the fundamental prerequisite of due process in any Certificate of

Convenience and Necessity (“CCN”) proceeding is that all potentially affected landowners must

receive actual, individual notice.4 Because a 765-kV line requires vastly expanded right-of-way

corridors and creates a significantly broader footprint of physical, visual, and environmental

impact than standard lines, the universe of legally affected parties expands exponentially. Yet,

due to the chaotic nature of mapping an unprecedented multi-county project on a compressed

timeline, critical notice failures have occurred. It is a matter of record in this proceeding that a

substantial number of landowners whose properties sit directly within or immediately adjacent

to the proposed routing corridors simply did not receive notice.5 Proceeding with a docket of

this magnitude while wholly bypassing the constitutional and statutory notification rights of

essential property owners renders any eventual regulatory decision void ab initio.

         Additionally, the justification for this rushed administrative timeline relies entirely on

House Bill 5066, passed during the 88th Legislative Session, which reduced the Commission’s



nature of the case"); Mitchell v. MAP Resources, Inc., 649 S.W.3d 180 (Tex. 2022) (emphasized that notice must be
"reasonably calculated, under all the circumstances, to apprise interested parties of the pendency of the action").
4
   Mullane v. Cent. Hanover Bank & Trust Co., 339 U.S. 306, 314 (1950) (holding that individual notice is a
foundational requirement of due process for any proceeding affecting property rights); see also 16 Tex. Admin. Code
§ 22.52 (requiring direct, individual mailed notice to all owners of land directly affected by a proposed transmission
line route); When an agency fails to guarantee this actual notice, it runs afoul of the constitutional protections guarding
private property. See Mitchell v. MAP Res., Inc., 649 S.W.3d 180, 188 (Tex. 2022).
5
  PFD at 36.

                                                            3
 project review window to an aggressive 180 days. However, the application of this accelerated

timeline to the 765-kV buildout is legally flawed because the legislative and executive

authorities responsible for the bill have explicitly confirmed that the scope of HB 5066 did not

contemplate or include extra-high-voltage projects of this magnitude. As confirmed by Texas

lawmakers and reinforced in an amicus curiae brief submitted by Texas Attorney General Ken

Paxton, the text of HB 5066 makes absolutely no mention of 765-kV lines. The primary author

of the bill and over 30 state legislators have formally stated that the statute was intended to direct

localized regional reliability studies and community-level infrastructure upgrades, not a multi-

billion dollar statewide transmission grid expansion. Furthermore, the Legislative Budget

Board’s fiscal note for HB 5066 projected zero anticipated financial impacts to the state or

consumers, proving that neither the Legislature, the relevant committees, nor the Governor had

notice of the massive economic scale now tied to the implementation of this plan.6

        By applying a statutory 180-day deadline designed for localized upgrades to an

unprecedented statewide megaproject, landowners who did receive notice have been left with

fewer than 90 days to defend their property rights against complex routing networks, while

others were entirely excluded from the process. The PFD acknowledges these exact systemic

notice failures, concluding that the rushed timeline made a mockery of public participation and



6
  Brief of Ken Paxton, Attorney General of Texas, as Amicus Curiae in Support of American Stewards of Liberty,
Inc.’s Motion to Defer Determination of Need at 1, 7–11, Joint Application of Oncor Electric Delivery Co. LLC &
LCRA Transmission Services Corp., PUC Docket No. 59475 (Aug. 28, 2026); Legislative Budget Board, Fiscal Note,
Tex. H.B. 5066, 88th Leg., R.S. (May 2023); Letter from State Senator Peter Flores & State Representatives Brad
Buckley, Hillary Hickland, Ellen Troxclair, and Terry Wilson, Joint Application of Oncor Electric Delivery Co. LLC
& LCRA Transmission Services Corp., PUC Docket No. 59475 (May 22, 2026) (Filing Item No. 5049); Amicus Curiae
Brief of Forty-Three Members of the Texas Legislature in Support of American Stewards of Liberty’s Motion to Defer
Determination of Need, PUC Docket No. 59475 (June 15, 2026) (Filing Item No. 6139); Statement of State
Representative Shelby Slawson, Representative Brad Buckley, et al., Urging Denial of Applications, PUC Docket No.
59475 / SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349 (Aug. 20, 2026); Statement of Dan Patrick, Lieutenant Governor of Texas,
Regarding ERCOT’s 765-kV Transmission Plan and Private Property Rights (July 31, 2026); Letter from State Senator
Charles Schwertner, Chairman, Senate Comm. on Business & Commerce, to Pub. Util. Comm’n of Tex., Urging
Denial of 765-kV Transmission Line Applications (July 31, 2026).

                                                        4
 recommending a total rejection of the applications due to the utilities' failure to provide due

process to affected citizens. Because the Texas Attorney General and state lawmakers have

verified that the statutory compression of the review period was never intended for projects of

this scope, and because the rushed implementation resulted in a total failure to notify all affected

landowners, forcing this docket forward under the accelerated HB 5066 framework constitutes

a clear violation of due process.7 The Commission should defer any further determination of

need or routing adjustments until the Texas Legislature has an opportunity to review the true

scope of the plan, establish necessary policy guardrails, and restore lawful administrative due

process.

           C.       Applicants’ position on Notice Requirements under 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(3)

                    1.       “Current county tax rolls” is undefined, and no evidence

                             establishes that the date Applicants used was not correct.8

                    2.       To support its notice efforts in this case, Applicants use the

                             Commission’s recent declination to adopt the Office of Public

                             Utility Counsel’s proposed change to 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(3) to

                             mirror the Texas Water Code, which requires Applicants to

                             provide notice to owners “according to the most current tax

                             appraisal rolls of the applicable central appraisal district at the time

                             the utility commission received the application for the certificate

                             or amendment. Applicants went further to share the Commission’s




7
    Id.
8
    Applicants’ Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision at 54-55.

                                                           5
                           statement that it “is not aware of any issues with the current notice

                          process that warrants such a revision.”9

        D.       The Mewhinney Family’s Reply

        Applicants’ reliance on historical inaction is a flawed defense. Applicants mistakenly

argue that because the Commission did not previously adopt a proposed Texas Water

Commission notice rule, the current notice process must be sufficient. A past decision not to

change a rule does not mean the rule works well in every situation. The Commission's previous

lack of awareness about notice issues does not mean those issues do not exist today; those issues

are very obvious in this case.

        Here, this is especially true for an unprecedented $2+ billion, 765-kV transmission line

project, which thoroughly demonstrates the serious issues with the current notice process. The

sheer volume of intervention requests, protests, and public confusion in this docket directly

contradicts Applicants’ claims. This case alone has exposed major flaws in the current system.

The Commission can and should address notice deficiencies under the Public Utility Regulatory

Act (“PURA”). The Commission is not trapped by past decisions. Under PURA, the

Commission must ensure a fair process that protects due process rights.

        The Applicants defense of their notice process relies on a dangerous premise: that

constitutional due process is a technicality that can be satisfied by simply checking a box.

Compliance with the bare minimum letter of a rule does not mean that Applicants have provided

meaningful or legally sufficient notice.10 When a project introduces an unprecedented 765-kV




9
  Id. at 56-57.
10
   Mitchell v. MAP Res., Inc., 649 S.W.3d 180, 188 (Tex. 2022) (holding that due process requires active diligence
rather than reliance on passive technicalities); Jones v. Flowers, 547 U.S. 220, 226 (2006) (ruling that literal
compliance with statutory notice procedures is insufficient if those procedures fail to provide actual notice).
Univ. of Tex. Med. Sch. at Houston v. Than, 901 S.W.2d 926, 930 (Tex. 1995) (emphasizing that due course of law

                                                        6
 transmission line spanning over a dozen counties, notice cannot be treated as a routine

bureaucratic exercise.11 The purpose of notice is to inform affected citizens so they can protect

their property rights. By treating notice as a task to be checked off a list rather than an active

obligation to inform, Applicants left thousands of Texas landowners in the dark.12

        The State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) Administrative Law Judges have

already recommended against administrative approval. This recommendation is a clear sign that

the application and its process are deeply flawed. The Commission cannot ignore the clear notice

issues raised in this docket just because it didn't address them in the past. The outpour of public

opposition and subsequent state legislative hearings confirm that this is not an isolated

complaint. The public was not properly notified, and a mechanical compliance defense cannot

cure a systemic failure of due process.

        Applicants’ attempt to dismiss valid notice concerns based on past inaction ignores the

widespread confusion and unfairness in this case. As noted by the Administrative Law Judges,

the evidence in this case proves that the current notice process fails to protect Texas landowners.

Accordingly, the Mewhinney Family requests that the Commission reject Applicants’

arguments, recognize these major notice flaws, and deny the Joint Application.

        Alternatively, when considering the administrative intent behind 16 TAC §22.52(a)(4)

the most accurate interpretation can be found within the provision itself: “Applicant must, on

the date it files an application, mail notice of its application to the owners of land, as stated on

the current county tax rolls, who would be directly affected by the requested certificate.”

According to the Applicants, the word “current” is vague or ambiguous, leading to their


11
   Univ. of Tex. Med. Sch. at Houston v. Than, 901 S.W.2d 926, 930 (Tex. 1995) (emphasizing that due course of law
is flexible and must scale with the gravity of the proceeding).
12
   Mullane v. Cent. Hanover Bank & Trust Co., 339 U.S. 306, 315 (1950) (holding that notice cannot be a "mere
gesture" but must reflect a genuine, active effort to inform).

                                                        7
 interpretation that “current” can mean days, weeks, or months beforehand. In the Fact Finding

section of the PFD, it states that over three dozen directly affected landowners were entitled to

notice according to current county tax rolls but were not properly notified as required in

accordance with 16 TAC §22.52(a)(4) due to Applicants utilizing old county tax rolls. The

Meriam Dictionary states that the definition for “current” is: occurring in or existing at the

present time; presently elapsing; or most recent.13

           According to the Finding of Facts in the PFD, Applicants acknowledge they did not use

the most recent county tax rolls related to the application date and even argues that using the

most recent county tax rolls would be close to impossible to facilitate. Thus, the portion of the

definition of current for “most recent” has not been reached.

           In the Finding of Facts in the PFD, the ALJs acknowledge that Applicants utilized a time

staggered method in order to procure the county tax rolls on a county by county basis. The

timeframe began on December 8, 2025 through February 15, 2026. The Applicants failed to

provide notice based on current county tax rolls that aligns with the “presently elapsing” day,

month, or year, thus, the portion of the definition of “presently elapsing” current has not been

reached.

           The PFD notes in the Finding of Facts, that the “appraisal districts update their rolls

continuously throughout the year.” In order for the first portion of the “current” definition to be

satisfied, the current county tax rolls would have to be utilized on the same day the Application

was filed in order for the “occurring in or existing at the present time” to apply. This was not

the case.



13
     CURRENT DEFINITION & MEANING - MERRIAM-WEBSTER, https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/current (last
        visited Sep 9, 2026).


                                                       8
             Therefore, according to the plain language of TAC § 22.52(a)(3) and in conjunction

with the different definitions of “current,” Applicants have failed to prove they provided proper

notice in accordance with TAC § 22.52(a)(3). Additionally, Applicants show that they had the

ability to pull records as recently as February 23, 2026 for some counties, but failed to utilize

this mechanism across the board to create less likelihood of prejudice against property-owners

from counties that were pulled before February 23, 2026. This time staggered method certainly

presents the perspective that Applicants utilized more “current” county tax rolls for some

counties, while utilizing past or old “current” county tax rolls for other counties.

            Should the Commission disagree with the interpretation brought forth in this section

related to the term “current”, the Mewhinney Family is gravely concerned for the future

precedence that could be created by this case related to the terminology of “current” and how

retroactively it could be applied.

II.        Reply to Exceptions to Findings of Noncompliance with Public Meeting Notice
           Requirements

           A.       The Commission Staff’s and Applicants’ position on Notice Requirements
                    under 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4)

                    1.       The Commission cannot hold a utility responsible, nor are the

                             Applicants solely responsible, for not taking actions that go beyond

                             what is required in a statute or rule and what precedence indicates

                             is acceptable.14

           B.       The Mewhinney Family’s Reply

           Commission Staff erroneously argues that under 16 TAC §22.52(a)(4), the Commission

cannot hold a utility responsible for failing to take actions that go beyond the explicit, bare-



14
     Commission Staff’s Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision at 8

                                                           9
 minimum wording of an administrative rule or historical precedent. This rigid interpretation

fundamentally misunderstands both the purpose of the Commission’s regulatory authority and the

core requirements of due process. The opposition attempts to insulate Applicants’ minimal notice

efforts by relying on PUC Docket No. 38597.15 This reliance is deeply flawed. Those cases

involved vastly different, more manageable parameters, making them legally and factually distinct

from the massive scale of the current proceeding.

        The quantitative data from the Commission’s own archives destroys any comparison

Applicants attempt to make. In Docket No. 38597, the public only had to digest 22 alternative

route options.16 To argue that a notice process designed for 22 options can seamlessly handle 122

entirely new alternative routes spanning hundreds of miles is mathematically and logistically

absurd. When the complexity of a project multiplies by more than 500%, a utility cannot claim

that 'standard precedent' protects them from a clear failure to provide meaningful notice.

        Further, Commission Staff's reliance on Docket No. 38597 as standard precedent for notice

sufficiency is legally disingenuous. That proceeding was governed by unique, highly compressed

regulatory constraints that are entirely absent here. Mandated CREZ Deadlines fourd in Docket

No. 38597 was a Competitive Renewable Energy Zone (CREZ) project.17 The Texas Legislature

placed these projects under explicit, fast-tracked legislative mandates to rush wind energy

transmission to metropolitan markets.18 The lack of additional public hearings or expanded notice

intervals in Docket No. 38597 was not an endorsement of a "minimalist notice standard." Rather,

it was a direct consequence of a statewide statutory urgency that forced the Commission to limit




15
   Commission Staff’s Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision, footnote 12.
16
   Id.
17
    Application of Oncor Elec. Delivery Co., LLC, Docket No. 38597, Pub. Util. Comm’n of Tex. (Final Order, Apr.
2011).
18
   Tex. Util. Code Ann. § 39.904(g).

                                                      10
 standard procedural timelines to prevent catastrophic delays to the CREZ buildout.19

        Here, the reality is exactly the opposite. While the past CREZ projects operated under an

explicit legislative mandate, this case presents the exact opposite dynamic. Applicants cannot

claim their massive 765-kV rollout is justified by standard “statutory urgency,” because Texas’s

highest executive and legislative officials have explicitly stated that this ultra-high-voltage

buildout was never authorized by the Legislature. In formal briefs filed before the Commission,

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton explicitly noted that no version of House Bill 5066—the law

Applicants claim drives this reliability plan—contains any mention whatsoever of 765-kV lines.20

The Attorney General confirmed that no legislator, committee, or the Governor had adequate

notice of the massive, unvetted cost and scope tied to this unauthorized project expansion.21 The

Lieutenant Governor's Direct Directive: Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, along with the Senate Committee

on Business and Commerce, has forcefully called on the Commission to halt and reject these

pending 765-kV applications.22 The state’s leadership has directly made it clear that the Legislature

must first reform the CCN process to guarantee fair, transparent treatment of landowners before

any such project proceeds. Over 40 members of the Texas House of Representatives, including

House Representative Brad Buckley (the primary author of the underlying legislation), have

formally informed the Commission that this multi-billion dollar project goes far beyond the

original intent of the law.23 The lawmakers confirmed that the statutory timelines in HB 5066 were

20
   Brief of Ken Paxton, Attorney General of Texas, as Amicus Curiae in Support of American Stewards of Liberty,
Inc.’s Motion to Defer Determination of Need at 1, 7–11, Joint Application of Oncor Electric Delivery Co. LLC &
LCRA Transmission Services Corp., PUC Docket No. 59475 (Aug. 28, 2026).
21
   Id.
22
   Statement of Dan Patrick, Lieutenant Governor of Texas, Regarding ERCOT’s 765-kV Transmission Plan and
Private Property Rights (July 31, 2026). [1.4.4]Letter from State Senator Charles Schwertner, Chairman, Senate
Comm. on Business & Commerce, to Pub. Util. Comm’n of Tex., Urging Denial of 765-kV Transmission Line
Applications (July 31, 2026).
23
   Amicus Curiae Brief of Forty-Three Members of the Texas Legislature in Support of American Stewards of
Liberty’s Motion to Defer Determination of Need, PUC Docket No. 59475 (June 15, 2026) (Filing Item No. 6139)

                                                      11
 meant for localized upgrades—not to serve as a back-door mechanism for running unvetted 765-

kV corridors across dozens of counties without public input.24

         The Commission cannot take a “procedural shortcut” born out of a specific 2010 CREZ

emergency and turn it into a permanent excuse to block public hearings and notice in Docket No.

59475. Because state leaders have uniformly confirmed that there is no legislative authorization—

much less an emergency mandate—for a 765-kV network, the regular, full demands of

constitutional due process must be upheld. Furthermore, and importantly, PURA does not limit the

Commission’s oversight to a passive checklist. While 16 TAC § 25.52 outlines standard quality

and operational service mandates, it serves as a regulatory floor, not a ceiling. The Commission is

explicitly charged with ensuring that public utilities operate in a manner that protects the public

interest, equity, and constitutional right.25 Accordingly, the Mewhinney Family requests that the

Commission reject Applicants’ arguments, recognize these major notice flaws, and deny the Joint

Application.

 III.    Reply to Exceptions to Findings of Need

         A.       The Commission Staff’s and Applicants’ position on Need

                  1.        The Commission broadly determined need in other dockets, namely

                            Docket 59315, and therefore it is logical for the Administrative Law

                            Judges to conclude that ERCOT’s recommendation for Import Path 2 is

                            needed.26

   Id.
25

utility regulation); Pub. Util. Comm’n of Tex. v. City of Austin, 728 S.W.2d 907, 919 (Tex. 1987) (affirming the
Commission’s primary statutory mandate to act as a guardian of the public interest); Tex. Dep't of Ins. v. Reconveyance
Servs., Inc., 306 S.W.3d 256, 258–59 (Tex. 2010).
26
   Commission Staff’s Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision at 9; Applicants’ Exceptions to the Proposal for
Decision at 7.

                                                           12
                     2.       The PFD’s notation that no representative of ERCOT testified on

                             necessity should be disregarded because the Commission “will give great

                             weight” to ERCOT’s recommendations regardless of the format of the

                             evidence and “requiring ERCOT to provide testimony for its

                             recommendations to be properly afforded great weight undermines the

                             purpose of the rule, which is to assess ERCOT recommendations that give

                             rise to CCN applications.”27

                    3.       The PFD improperly misconstrues Commission Staff’s witness, John

                             Poole’s expert opinion that a “re-evaluation of load demand might be

                             useful.” 28

           B.       The Mewhinney Family’s Reply

           Commission Staff argues that the Administrative Law Judges’ Proposal for Decision

(PFD) should disregard the fact that no representative of the Electric Reliability Council of

Texas (ERCOT) testified regarding the necessity of this project. Staff claims that under the

Commission's rules, ERCOT’s recommendations are automatically entitled to “great weight”

regardless of evidentiary format, and that requiring formal testimony would “undermine the

purpose of the rule.” This argument is a dangerous mischaracterization of Texas administrative

law and the rules of evidence.

           “Great weight” does not equal “unquestioned immunity” from cross-examination.

Commission Staff attempts to transform a regulatory guideline into an absolute shield against

evidentiary scrutiny, which actually raises the question of reliability the Commission affords

under the unvetted “great weight.” While the Commission may give weight to ERCOT's


27
     Commission Staff’s Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision at 10-11.
28
     Commission Staff’s Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision at 11.

                                                          13
 structural recommendations, that weight cannot be granted blindly in a contested case hearing.29

Giving "great weight" to an unvetted, untested piece of paper—while denying Intervenors the

constitutional right to cross-examine the authors of that data—constitutes a fundamental

violation of due process and the Texas Administrative Procedure Act (APA).30

        Additionally, an unprecedented $2+ billion project requires admissible proof, not

assumed deference. Otherwise, why hold a hearing at all? When an applicant seeks a CCN for

a project of this historic scale, “necessity” is a core statutory element that must be proven by a

preponderance of competent evidence. ERCOT's recommendation is a starting point, not the

final word. By choosing not to present an ERCOT representative to sit on the witness stand,

Applicants and Staff denied the ALJs, the public, and affected landowners the ability to test the

underlying modeling, load growth assumptions, and technical data used to justify slicing a 765-

kV corridor across Texas.

        Further, staff's reliance on untested recommendations fails in light of unrebutted expert

testimony to the contrary. Staff's argument relies entirely on the fiction that an unvetted ERCOT

endorsement creates an irrebuttable presumption of necessity.31 It does not. In this proceeding,

Intervenors introduced sworn expert testimony directly contradicting ERCOT’s conclusions.32

This expert testimony actively dismantled Applicants’ necessity claims by exposing flawed

load-growth projections, showing that alternative lower-voltage options were completely

ignored, and proving that a 765-kV rollout is an overbuilt, premature solution. The Commission

presumptions cannot insulate data from evidentiary scrutiny).
30

Comm’n of Tex. v. Constellation Energy Commodities Grp., Inc., 351 S.W.3d 588, 595 (Tex. App.—Austin 2011, pet.
denied) (affirming that agency rules cannot override the statutory requirements of the APA); In re H.E.B. Grocery
Co., L.P., 492 S.W.3d 300, 304–05 (Tex. 2016) (holding that the denial of cross-examination on critical, rights-
affecting data violates basic due process guarantees).
31
   Commission Staff’s Exceptions to the Proposal for Decisions, Article III., Exceptions to Determination of Need
32
   Proposal for Decision at 172, Findings of Fact Nos. 68-148 and Proposed Conclusion of Law No. 14.

                                                        14
 cannot legally accord "great weight" to an absent, un-cross-examined ERCOT report when the

only live, admissible expert testimony on the witness stand systematically proved that no such

necessity exists.

         Insultingly, staff’s position invents a unilateral exemption to the Texas Rules of

Evidence. Staff’s assertion that requiring ERCOT to provide actual testimony "undermines the

purpose of the rule" is legally absurd. No Commission rule can override state law regarding

contested hearings.33 Under Texas law, statements contained in unvetted reports are hearsay

when introduced to prove the truth of the matter asserted. The ALJs in the PFD correctly noted

the total absence of ERCOT testimony because, without a live witness subject to cross-

examination, there is no legally sufficient evidentiary foundation to overcome the specific expert

testimony submitted by Intervenors.34 The Commission cannot allow Staff to substitute lazy

bureaucratic deference for actual, cross-examined proof. Because ERCOT refused to stand

behind its recommendations under oath, and because Intervenors provided compelling expert

testimony to the contrary, the ALJs correctly determined that necessity was not legally

established.35

         Moreover, Commission Staff improperly suggests that the ALJs and the Commission

can establish the statutory “need” for the 765-kV infrastructure in Docket No. 59475 by simply

looking to the determination of need made in a completely separate proceeding. This cross-case

bootstrapping is legally misguided and represents a severe breach of administrative procedure.



33
   Tex. R. Evid. 801(d), 802; see also Tex. Gov't Code Ann. § 2001.081 (mandating that the rules of evidence applied
in civil district courts govern contested cases before state agencies).
34
   Tex. Dep't of Pub. Safety v. Caruana, 363 S.W.3d 558, 564–565 (Tex. 2012) (holding that unsworn, un-cross-
examined hearsay reports are legally insufficient to support an administrative finding when confronted with contrary
evidence).
35
   City of Keller v. Wilson, 168 S.W.3d 802, 822–23 (Tex. 2005) (holding that a regulatory finder of fact cannot legally
credit evidence that lacks a proper foundation or ignore uncontroverted live expert proof).


                                                          15
          Every CCN application must stand on its own record. Under PURA and the Texas

Administrative Procedure Act (APA), a CCN application must be evaluated strictly on the

        Commission Staff argues that the Administrative Law Judges' Proposal for Decision

law and the rules of evidence.

Commission Staff attempts to transform a regulatory guideline into an absolute shield against
